critique:
field method, ANNOTATOR PROMPT
  The way the demonstration moved the cube, fixed at the first decision step from the demonstration steps and copied unchanged at every later step. Decide it from the TRANSPORT frames of the demonstration, meaning the frames in which the cube is moving toward the target, and from whether the gripper ever rises off the table (height above about 0.08) with something held, never from a single finger reading during the closing motion. Write `push` when, in the transport frames, the fingers read about 0% (closed on nothing) and the gripper height stays at table level (below about 0.04) throughout, and nothing is ever marked as held while the gripper is raised; this is `push` even if the gripper descended next to the stick, the fingers passed through a reading of roughly 19-30% for one frame while closing before reaching 0%, the stick's head was listed near the gripper, or the stick ended up shoved to a new spot as the gripper swept past it. Write `hook` when the fingers settle at about 20-25% and stay there through the transport frames, the stick is marked as held in the gripper, and the gripper rises well above the table (height above about 0.08) with the stick before coming down to drag the cube. Write `pick` when the fingers settle at about 40-60%, the cube is marked as held, the gripper rises well above the table with it, and the cube is released over the target. A reading of 19-30% that is immediately followed by 0% is a closing transient, not a grasp. e.g. push

field method, POLICY PROMPT
  The way the demonstration moved the cube. Fill it at the first decision step from the demonstration steps and copy it unchanged at every later step; never write `unknown` after the first step. Do not decide from the first frame in which the fingers close; look at the frames in which the cube is sliding or carried toward the target and at the greatest height the gripper reaches while anything is held. `push`: in those transport frames the fingers read about 0% and the gripper height stays below about 0.04 the whole time, and nothing is ever marked as held while the gripper is raised. A one-frame finger reading of roughly 19-30% that drops to 0% at the next frame is just the fingers closing on nothing; it does not make a hook, even if the gripper came down beside the stick, the stick's head is listed next to the gripper, or the stick is in a different place at the end because the gripper pushed it aside. `hook`: the fingers settle at about 20-25% and stay there through the transport frames, the stick is explicitly marked as held in the gripper, and the gripper rises above about 0.08 carrying the stick before dragging the cube. `pick`: the fingers settle at about 40-60%, the cube is explicitly marked as held, the gripper rises above about 0.08 with it, and the cube is released over the target. e.g. push

the policy prompt for subgoal
  The failure was at the first decision step of a push demonstration in which the gripper happened to come down beside the stick: the fingers showed a roughly 19% reading for one frame while closing, then 0% at table height, and the cube slid to the target while the stick was nudged aside. The policy wrote `hook` and chose A (pick up the peg) where the recorded subgoal was C (push). This breaks PREDICTABILITY of `method` (the instruction let a closing transient count as a hook grasp) and so SUFFICIENCY of the first subgoal. The subgoal rules themselves need two changes. First, the rule that chooses by `method` at the first decision step must say that `method` is decided from the transport frames and the maximum raised height, as the memory instruction now states, so that a push demonstration that brushed the stick still yields C. Second, the later-step rules currently tell the policy to judge the fingers and rise alone and treat the scene as sufficient, which is why `method` was carried and never read; replace them with: at every later decision step read `method` first and use the scene only to locate the position in that method's chain. If `method` is `hook`: fingers at about 20-25% and gripper risen after a descent onto the stick -> B; otherwise (fingers fully open or at 0%, nothing raised) -> A. If `method` is `pick`: fingers at about 40-60% and risen after a descent onto the cube -> E; otherwise -> D. If `method` is `push`: C in every situation. Keep the guard that B and E are never chosen without the matching finger opening and rise. Drop the sentence that says the marking of an object as held is unreliable and should be ignored; the marking is one of the cues that separates hook from push. The `method` field is kept: it is the only record of the demonstration and is what decides between A, D and C whenever a grasp closes on nothing or reopens, and under the rewritten rules it is read at every later step rather than only inferred from the scene.

critiques.recorded: C: close gripper and push the cube to the target
critiques.missing_from_policy_prompt_for_memory: It did not say that a transient finger reading of about 19-25% seen mid-closure (t=64) does not count as a hook grasp when the fingers go on to reach 0% at the next step (t=80) while the gripper stays at table height (0.02-0.03); fingers reaching 0% means nothing is held, so the method is push even if the gripper first descended near the stick and the stick ends up displaced (from [87,171] to [103,130]) as the gripper swept past it. It also did not say that `hook` requires the stick to be explicitly marked as held (and fingers to stay at ~20-25% throughout the drag), and that a stick simply being nudged aside while the cube slides to the target is a push.
